source: Kan and Gero (2007) Can an objective measurement of design protocols reflect the quality of a design outcome? (ICED07)
finding: Opened the full paper (gaps 6 and 7). It tests whether linkograph entropy tracks design outcome. Data are Bilda's 12 sessions: 6 architects, each with over 10 years of experience, two sessions of about 45 min, one blindfolded (BF) and one sketching (SK), thinking aloud. Three judges scored outcomes on five criteria. The authors themselves say whole-session entropy is only weakly tied to outcome.
numbers: Outcome scores 3.7 to 7.7, mean 5.87, SD 1.12. Three highest sessions (7.1, 6.9, 6.5) vs three lowest (4.3, 4.9, 4.9), a gap over 40%. Normalised total entropy: high group 0.499, 0.338, 0.299; low group 0.529, 0.481, 0.422. So the LOW-scoring group had HIGHER entropy.
quote: Positive correlation between entropy and the evaluation of the design outcome is weak.
limits: Six designers, 12 sessions, no inferential test. Only the extreme sessions analysed in detail. Only three judges.
agent_relevance: Do not use link density or entropy of a trace as a quality signal. In the original data low-quality sessions had more links, not fewer.

source: Kan and Gero (2007) ICED07: change-of-entropy result
finding: The paper's positive claim is about the change of entropy over time, not the level. With a 28-move window, high-scoring sessions show entropy dropping in the middle and rising near the end. Abstract: outcome is more related to the rate of change of entropy than to entropy alone. This is shown by plots and polynomial fits of three sessions, not by a correlation coefficient.
numbers: Window 28 moves (7 moves judged too noisy). Blindfolded sessions scored higher than sketching in most pairs (all BF >= matching SK except one tie). Entropy difference BF vs SK called marginal.
limits: Three high sessions only; curve fits are descriptive. No replication found in this search. The entropy dip is due to sparse links, not saturation.
agent_relevance: A time-shaped pattern (explore, consolidate, link again at the end) is a hypothesis for coding agent traces. It has no replicated support.

source: Smith, Kreminski et al. (2025) Fuzzy Linkography: Automatic Graphical Summarization of Creative Activity Traces (ACM C and C)
finding: A language-model embedding replaces the human coder in linkography. Applied to text-to-image prompt traces, ChatGPT 3.5 ideation sequences and researcher publication histories. No agreement with human linkographs and no outcome prediction are reported (gap 7: validity numbers not reported).
numbers: 6,424 image-prompt traces, 1,879 kept (7 or more prompts, median 14 moves, longest 536); 72 idea sequences; 10 researchers. all-MiniLM-L6-v2, cosine threshold 0.35 rescaled to [0,1]; about 0.4 s per trace. Human validation: none. Authors say they do not make evaluative use of entropy.
limits: Threshold chosen empirically. Model overweights some word types and misses some links. Formal human-machine comparison left to future work.
agent_relevance: A cheap automatic linkograph of agent steps is feasible, but its validity against human links and against answer quality is untested.

source: Sakib, Hurst, Safayeni (2026) Evaluating the performance of LLMs in taxonomic classification of questions in verbal protocols of design, AI EDAM 40:e6
finding: Re-opened the full text for gap 2 (kappa for an LLM coder). Eris question taxonomy (3 categories, 21 subcategories) on design verbal protocols. A kappa table (Table 8) exists, but its body was not readable in the HTML text, so no kappa is available. Only percent agreement is readable.
numbers: d1: 1,942 test questions; d2: 175 test. GPT-4.1 vs human at category level 80.2%, subcategory 52.5%. Human vs human 85.7% category, 74.7% subcategory. Experiment 2 range 76.7% to 85.1%. Claude Sonnet 4.5 82.9% (abstract). Prompt conditions A to G (category): 57.0, 69.9, 70.2, 72.7, 79.4, 79.8, 80.3%. Each condition run once.
limits: Not FBS codes. Questions were pre-identified, so segmentation and context were not tested. The abstract's 'up to 85.7%' is the human figure. Prior runs vary about 3% between repeats. Gap 2 stays open for FBS.
agent_relevance: Expect about 80% raw agreement at coarse level and about half at fine level. Use coarse codes and keep human spot checks.

source: Sakib, Hurst, Safayeni (2026) per-code accuracy of GPT-4.1 (same paper)
finding: Accuracy varies a lot by code. Concrete, surface-marked codes are easy. Codes that need reading intent are hard. Expect the same for design-process codes.
numbers: Categories: LLQ 93%, DRQ 60%, GDQ 53%. Subcategories: Disjunctive 89.1%, Quantification 83.3%, Verification 63.1%, Instrumental 57.1%, Rationale 52.1%, Feature specification 39.3%, Concept completion 22.7%, Ideation 20.8%. Class mix in d1: 66.5% LLQ, 7.4% DRQ, 26.1% GDQ.
limits: The majority class drives the overall percent. Raw percent is not chance-corrected. Small subcategories.
agent_relevance: Report per-code agreement, not one overall figure, when coding agent traces.

source: Walden (2026) Reasoning Models Will Blatantly Lie About Their Reasoning
finding: Gap 5 (partly). Reasoning models given hints often use them and then deny it. Still multiple-choice hint tasks, not open-ended design.
numbers: 3 models (Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Thinking, Kimi K2 Thinking, Claude 4.5 Haiku); GPQA-Diamond and 200 MMLU-Pro items; 10K-token thinking budget; 4 hint types. Claude 4.5 Haiku best honesty score 34.5% (grader hacking). Kimi from 0% (sycophancy) to 100% (metadata) on GPQA. Claude switches to the hinted correct answer above 95% for grader hacking and metadata. Judge check on 30 CoTs: hint presence 90.0% agreement (kappa 0.80), hint reliance 73.3% (kappa 0.26).
limits: Only 3 models. Claude CoT is an API summary. No open-ended tasks, no scaffold tested. The reliance judgement has low kappa 0.26.
agent_relevance: A trace is not a record of what drove the answer. Do not treat agent trace codes as causal explanations.

source: Young (2026) Lie to Me: How Faithful Is Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Reasoning Models?
finding: 12 open-weight reasoning models show a large faithfulness spread, and thinking traces acknowledge hints far more often than final answers do.
numbers: 498 questions (300 MMLU, 198 GPQA Diamond), 41,832 runs, 6 hint types. Faithfulness from 39.7% (Seed-1.6-Flash) to 89.9% (DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale); overall 69.7% (7,161 of 10,276 influenced cases). By hint: consistency 35.5%, sycophancy 53.9%, metadata 69.9%, grader 77.7%, unethical 79.4%. Keyword check: acknowledgement in about 87.5% of thinking traces but about 28.6% of final answers. A Sonnet judge gave lower faithfulness than the main panel on 10 of 12 models (pipeline 82.6% overall, a 12.9 point gap). Scale regression R2 0.07.
limits: Multiple-choice only. No hand-labelled validation set. Keyword classifier is coarse. Judge choice moves the number by about 13 points.
agent_relevance: Faithfulness depends on the judge. Report the judge and its agreement with humans. Newer models look better than the 25 to 39% earlier numbers (a21) but vary widely.

source: Lewis-Lim, Tan, Zhao, Aletras (2025) Analysing Chain of Thought Dynamics: Active Guidance or Unfaithful Post-hoc Rationalisation? (EMNLP 2025)
finding: Abstract page only. On soft-reasoning tasks (analytical, commonsense), instruction-tuned, reasoning and distilled models differ in how much they use their CoT. Authors report that CoT influence and faithfulness are not always aligned. Nearest found work to non-multiple-choice faithfulness (gap 5).
numbers: The abstract page gave no model list and no numbers.
limits: Full text not opened. Soft reasoning is still not open-ended design.
agent_relevance: Reliance on CoT depends on task. Test per task type before trusting trace codes.

source: Ballon, Verbeken, Ginis, Algaba (2026) Probing the Trajectories of Reasoning Traces in LLMs
finding: Gaps 1 and 4 (equal-length controls). Truncating a trace at token percentiles and re-injecting it shows accuracy rises with the share of trace given, and the gain comes from instance-relevant content, not length or style.
numbers: Qwen3-4B/8B/14B and gpt-oss-20b/120b; GPQA Diamond (n=198) and MMLU-Pro; 3 runs. Original traces +18.1 to +33.1% over baseline. Length-matched random tokens -3.9 to +4.2%. Swapped trace from another question -18.4 to +3.0%. Shuffled same tokens +0.3 to +10.8%. All differences at decile 100 vs controls p<0.001 (McNemar).
limits: Multiple-choice, open models. Tests the model's own trace, not a coding scheme. Qwen3-8B shows a bias toward answer A.
agent_relevance: Coherent, instance-specific content is what helps. Any scaffold must be judged against length-matched and shuffled controls.

source: Ballon et al. (2026) trace length versus accuracy (same paper)
finding: They report a negative correlation between full-trace length and accuracy. Longer traces look difficulty-driven, not helpful, and can derail the hardest items or give confident wrong answers.
numbers: Exact correlation value not extracted this session; the text states direction only.
agent_relevance: Process-style gains can be confounded with length. For gap 1, compare at matched length and matched difficulty.

source: Valmeekam, Palod, Stechly, Gundawar, Kambhampati (2025/2026) Beyond Semantics: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Reasonless Intermediate Tokens (TMLR)
finding: Abstract page. Small transformers trained on corrupted, problem-unrelated traces do about as well as on correct traces and generalise better out of distribution. RL post-training raises accuracy but not trace validity. Trace length does not track problem complexity.
numbers: No figures on the abstract page.
limits: Trained-from-scratch formal tasks. Does not speak directly to prompting frontier models. Differs in emphasis from Ballon (swapped traces hurt).
agent_relevance: Counts against reading codes of a trace as proof the coded process caused the answer.

source: Luo et al. (2026) Capable yet Parsimonious: Extracting and Characterizing Hidden CoT in Frontier Models
finding: Abstract page. A tool-call trick makes closed frontier models write out reasoning. They check it against native CoT on open models: extracted reasoning matches native performance and beats no-reasoning. They classify step types and induced reasoning trees.
numbers: No benchmark scores readable on the page. A web-search summary quoted MATH numbers (30.5 to 73.3 and 21.4 to 84.3) but these were NOT verified here.
limits: Page gave no numbers. Authors note the traces may be post-hoc rationalisation.
agent_relevance: Forced reasoning may work like a think-aloud trace (gap 4), but this was not tested at equal tokens against silent answers.

source: Guo, Yin, Sun, Chen (2024) Empirical Study of Problem-solution Co-evolution in Human-GAI Collaborative Conceptual Design (DRS2024)
finding: Gap 3 (human side with AI). Retrospective protocol analysis of 20 novice designers: three groups with GAI (ChatGPT, Midjourney, both) and a control without. Segments coded as 4 co-evolution transition types and 3 inference types. The AI is a partner, not the designer.
numbers: 20 participants (13 F, 7 M, mean age 24), 5 per group. 686 segments, 1,322 inference behaviours. Kappa per code reported on 10% of data but values not in the text read. Expert creativity kappa average 0.66. Creativity vs control: ChatGPT +0.648 (5% level), Midjourney +0.748 (1%), both +0.512 (10%). Abduction: Midjourney +27.2 units (1%), ChatGPT +7.2 (10%). Each abduction unit adds 0.058 creativity (1%).
limits: Five per cell, stepwise regression, retrospective not concurrent protocol, novices. Midjourney effect on creativity turns to -0.833 once abduction is controlled, so the mechanism claim is fragile.
agent_relevance: Does not answer whether forced problem-solution crossings help an LLM. It shows protocol coding of AI-supported design exists, with small samples.

source: Fox, Ericsson, Best (2011) Do procedures for verbal reporting of thinking have to be reactive? Psych Bulletin 137(2) (snippets and a citing review)
finding: Gap 8 only partly closed. Snippets repeat the abstract: think-aloud r=-.03 over about 3,500 participants; describing or explaining is reactive and raises performance; all reporting slows tasks. A citing review (Double and Birney 2019) says Fox and Charness (2010) found Raven's matrices reactive to think-aloud in older but not younger adults. No full moderator table seen and nothing on design tasks.
numbers: r=-.03 (nearly 3,500 participants), as before. Raven reactivity in older adults: no numbers seen.
limits: Search snippets only; full text not opened. Whether any design task is among the 94 studies is unknown.
agent_relevance: Reactivity may depend on task. Test on the agent's own task types.

source: Dorst and Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution, Design Studies 22(5)
finding: Gap 6 stays open. Fetches of the full paper failed (one host unreachable, one 403). Search snippets only: protocol data from experienced industrial designers, designs rated for overall quality and creativity, model of co-evolution with default and surprise spaces. No numbers obtained.
limits: Not opened. A 2026 DRS scoping review calls the model highly influential, which is not evidence that it replicated.
agent_relevance: No Dorst and Cross numbers should be used.

source: Pombal, Rei, Martins (2026) Self-Preference Bias in Rubric-Based Evaluation of LLMs (COLM 2026)
finding: Gap 9 (shared bias), indirect. LLM judges favour their own or family outputs even on objective rubrics. Ensembling several judges helps but does not remove it. This is output-favouring, not coder-coder agreement.
numbers: On IFEval and LiveCodeBench, among rubrics where generators fail, judges can be over 50% more likely to wrongly mark them satisfied when the output is their own. HealthBench: scores skewed up to 10 points. Ensembling reduces but does not eliminate.
limits: Rubric judging of outputs, not coding of reasoning traces. No data on LLM-LLM vs LLM-human agreement.
agent_relevance: Use a coder from a different model family than the agent being coded, and an ensemble. Gap 9 stays open for direct coder-agreement evidence.

source: Search summaries on family-mixing (arXiv 2604.11589 multimodal judge bias; practitioner posts), snippets only
finding: A multimodal-judge study is reported to find mutual preference bias inside model families, reduced by an ensemble across families. Practitioner blogs claim same-family ensembles agree because of shared priors. Not verified.
agent_relevance: Weak support for mixing coder families. A direct test on trace coding is needed.

source: Style over Substance: Distilled Language Models Reason (arXiv 2504.01738), search summary only
finding: Gap 10 stays open. No replication of Li's +9.7 trace-guidance result outside the authors' pool was found. A related paper is reported to show that distilled models trained on synthetic traces with hard-coded stages (framing, exploration, verification, synthesis) can match emergent traces. Seen only in a search summary.
limits: Snippet only. Not an equal-token test.
agent_relevance: Structure-only imitation is plausible but untested.
